title: Accessibility as Practice
eyebrow: Inclusive interfaces · Preserve meaning, operation, and feedback for more people
summary: Learn accessibility as an engineering practice: start with semantic structure, make every task operable, expose names and state, test real journeys, and keep accessibility intact through production change.
prerequisites: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript is helpful because this guide uses native elements, styles, and interaction behavior.
Form and Input Handling is a useful continuation for accessible field names, errors, and submission states.
learningOutcomes: Explain accessibility as preserving perceivable information, operable controls, understandable behavior, and compatible structure across different needs and technologies.
Build interfaces that start with semantic HTML, support keyboard and zoom/reflow use, and expose names, roles, values, and state.
Test an accessibility journey with automated checks, manual keyboard review, assistive technology, and representative content without treating any single check as proof.

heroVisual.title: An accessible feature has several connected layers
heroVisual.caption: A visual style is only one layer; meaning, operation, feedback, and compatibility must remain available together.

nodes.label: Meaning
nodes.detail: Structure and text identify content and controls.

nodes.label: Perception
nodes.detail: Contrast, text alternatives, captions, and reflow preserve information.

nodes.label: Operation
nodes.detail: Keyboard, touch, and other input methods can complete the task.

nodes.label: Feedback
nodes.detail: Focus, errors, status, and state changes are exposed.

nodes.label: Compatibility
nodes.detail: Browsers and assistive technologies can interpret the interface.

sections.title: 1. Start with the task, not a compliance label
sections.summary: Accessibility asks whether people can perceive, operate, understand, and recover through the interfaces you ship.

blocks.text: A person may use a keyboard, screen reader, magnification, voice control, captions, a mobile device, high contrast settings, or a temporary limitation such as a broken arm or noisy room. The goal is not a special alternate page. The goal is that the same meaningful task—reading an article, submitting a form, or purchasing a ticket—remains possible through different ways of perceiving and interacting.

rows: Can the person perceive it?
Text alternatives, sufficient contrast, captions, and content that reflows.
Meaning exists only in color, an image, or audio.
Can the person operate it?
Keyboard focus, adequate target behavior, no keyboard trap, and enough time.
A custom control responds only to pointer events.
Can the person understand it?
Predictable labels, instructions, errors, and consistent navigation.
A field error says only 'invalid'.
Can technology interpret it?
Correct element semantics, names, roles, values, and state.
A clickable div has no button semantics.
blocks.caption: Use the user's task and observable evidence to guide decisions; a score alone cannot describe the experience.

blocks.prompt: If a page passes a color-contrast checker, is the whole task necessarily accessible?
blocks.explanation: Contrast covers one perception concern. The task may still fail because of missing semantics, keyboard operation, focus management, labels, errors, or dynamic announcements.

sections.title: 2. Let native semantics carry the first meaning
sections.summary: The browser's built-in elements provide names, roles, keyboard behavior, and relationships that custom widgets must otherwise recreate.

blocks.text: Use a heading for a heading, a button for an action, a link for navigation, a label for a field, and a list for a list. Semantic HTML gives browsers and assistive technology a shared interpretation. CSS can change appearance without changing that meaning. JavaScript should enhance a real control or implement a well-understood pattern only when native behavior cannot express the requirement.

blocks.code: Filter results
blocks.explanation: The button is already focusable and activatable. aria-expanded communicates the disclosure state, aria-controls names the controlled section, and hidden keeps the closed content out of the active interface. JavaScript must update both the visible state and aria-expanded together.

blocks.title: ARIA does not repair incorrect interaction
blocks.body: Accessible Rich Internet Applications (ARIA) can expose roles, names, and state, but it does not automatically supply keyboard behavior, focus movement, or correct event handling. Prefer native HTML and use ARIA to fill a real semantic gap.

sections.title: 3. Make every control operable and focusable
sections.summary: Keyboard support reveals whether the interface has a real interaction model rather than a pointer-only imitation.

blocks.title: Review one task with a keyboard

items.title: Reach the first control
items.explanation: Use Tab from the page start and confirm focus is visible and ordered by the task's meaning.
items.result: The interaction surface can be entered.

items.title: Operate each control
items.explanation: Use the expected keys for links, buttons, fields, menus, and dialogs; do not require a mouse gesture.
items.result: Each action has a keyboard path.

items.title: Track focus after change
items.explanation: When a dialog opens, an item is removed, or a validation result appears, keep focus on a meaningful next location.
items.result: The person does not lose context.

items.title: Escape and recover
items.explanation: Close temporary UI with its documented key, restore focus when appropriate, and ensure no focus trap remains.
items.result: The task has a complete exit path.

blocks.prompt: Is removing the browser focus outline an accessibility improvement if no replacement is provided?
blocks.explanation: Visible focus is evidence of where keyboard input will act. A custom indicator may work, but removing the only indicator leaves the person without that orientation.

sections.title: 4. Preserve information through text, contrast, and reflow
sections.summary: Information must survive different sizes, settings, and sensory channels.

blocks.text: Provide a useful text alternative for meaningful images and an empty alternative for decorative ones. Do not put essential instructions in color alone; pair status colors with words, icons, or structure. Text and controls need adequate contrast for the chosen visual treatment. Let content reflow and resize without forcing two-dimensional scrolling for ordinary reading, and respect user preferences such as reduced motion when animation is not essential.

rows: Meaningful image
Describe the information or function in alt text or nearby prose.
A non-visual reader receives the same purpose.
Decorative image
Use an empty alternative and keep it out of the reading path.
The decoration does not interrupt content.
Video or audio
Provide synchronized captions and a transcript when the content needs them.
Information is available without hearing the track.
Status or trend
Use text and structure in addition to color.
Color vision, forced colors, and narration do not erase meaning.
Animation
Offer reduced motion and avoid motion that distracts or causes harm.
The user retains control over a sensory effect.
blocks.caption: Choose the alternative from the information the media carries, not from its file format.

sections.title: 5. Name fields and expose state and feedback
sections.summary: A person needs to know what a control is, what value it has, what is required, and what changed after an action.

blocks.text: A visible label should be programmatically associated with its control. Instructions should appear before they are needed, and errors should identify the field, explain the problem, and state how to correct it. Dynamic status such as 'Saved' or '3 results' must be exposed without stealing focus unnecessarily. Preserve entered values when safe so recovery does not become a memory test.

blocks.code:
Use the format A1A 1A1.

Enter six characters, including the space.
blocks.explanation: The label supplies the name. aria-describedby connects help and error text so it can be discovered with the field. aria-invalid exposes the current error state; application logic should remove or update it when the value is corrected.

blocks.title: Do not announce every change
blocks.body: Use a status or live region for important asynchronous feedback, not for every keystroke. Excessive announcements make a task slower and harder to follow.

sections.title: 6. Respect settings, devices, and real content
sections.summary: Accessibility fails when a design works only at one viewport, pointer precision, font size, or ideal text length.

blocks.text: Test zoom, text-only enlargement, narrow and wide layouts, touch targets, long translations, empty states, errors, and forced-colors or high-contrast settings. Do not lock text to a fixed height, hide overflow that contains instructions, or rely on hover as the only way to reveal a control. A responsive layout should preserve reading order and task completion as its boxes rearrange.

blocks.title: Content-resilient interface checks
items: Headings and landmarks still form a meaningful outline when styles are disabled.
Long labels and translated text do not overlap controls or disappear behind clipping.
The interface remains usable at increased text size and browser zoom.
Hover-only information has a keyboard and touch equivalent.
Errors, loading, empty, and success states are tested rather than treated as exceptional decoration.

sections.title: 7. Test accessibility continuously and fix causes
sections.summary: Automated rules find patterns; human task testing finds whether the experience makes sense.

blocks.text: Run automated checks for detectable issues such as missing names, invalid relationships, and contrast where the tool can evaluate it. Then use keyboard-only journeys, browser accessibility trees, zoom and reflow review, and representative screen-reader testing. Test the task from entry to recovery, including a failed network request and a validation error. A conformance level is a target for a documented standard, not a guarantee that every person can complete every task.

rows: Control has no accessible name
Missing label, text, or valid naming relationship
Use native control semantics and a persistent label.
Keyboard focus disappears
DOM replacement or focus styling removed
Preserve focus intentionally and provide a visible indicator.
Screen reader announces stale state
Visual state changed without semantic state
Update the control's state and the controlled content together.
Automated test is green but task fails
Tool cannot judge sequence, clarity, or recovery
Reproduce the complete journey with keyboard and assistive technology.
blocks.caption: Fix the semantic or interaction cause rather than adding a local attribute until one checker turns green.

blocks.title: Definition of done
items: The task has a clear name, structure, operation path, feedback, and recovery path.
Manual keyboard review covers every meaningful state.
Representative content is tested at zoom, narrow width, and with settings that alter presentation.
Automated findings are triaged and recorded without treating the tool as the sole oracle.
Component changes include an accessibility regression check in the same test or review path.

glossary.definition: The practice of designing and building products so people with different abilities, devices, settings, and assistive technologies can perceive, operate, understand, and use them.
The text exposed to users and assistive technology as the identifying name of a control or other interface object.
Hardware or software such as screen readers, magnifiers, voice control, or alternative input that helps a person interact with digital content.
Accessible Rich Internet Applications, a set of attributes that communicates roles, states, and properties when native HTML does not express a needed interface pattern.
The current target for keyboard input and related interaction in a document.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, a W3C technical standard for making web content more accessible.
